name: Halo effect
statement: One favourable impression of a person spreads to judgements it has nothing to do with, so someone who looks the part is rated as more capable too.
meaning: The claim is about contamination between ratings that ought to be independent. If a rater scores a person on a list of separate qualities and every score moves with every other, either the qualities really do travel together in people, or the rater formed one overall impression and read it off once per line. Thorndike's argument was that the correlations were too high and too even to be the first. What makes the effect awkward to study is that this is a claim about the difference between real covariation and rated covariation, and measuring the real thing is exactly what the ratings were supposed to do.

origin.note: The paper is "A constant error in psychological ratings". Officers rated their subordinates on physical qualities, intelligence, leadership and personal qualities using a scale devised by Walter Dill Scott, whose instructions required each of the four to be judged independently. One flight commander rating 137 aviation cadets correlated intelligence with physique at .51, with leadership at .58 and with character at .64. Across the three raters Thorndike studied next, the average correlations were .31 for physique with intelligence, .39 for physique with leadership and .28 for physique with character. Those three figures are averages over raters, not single coefficients.

evidence: The original evidence is correlational and comes from rating data. Thorndike carried it into teaching through Knight's study of 129 teachers rated by a superior on the Boyce score card, where general merit correlated .68 with intellect, .79 with power in discipline and .63 with voice, and voice itself correlated .63 with intelligence. Nisbett and Wilson supplied the experimental version. They showed 118 University of Michigan undergraduates one of two seven-minute videotaped interviews with the same instructor, a Belgian who spoke English with a pronounced accent. In one interview he was warm and flexible, in the other cold and doctrinaire. Liking moved as intended, 5.48 against 3.18 on an eight-point scale, t = 8.62, p < .00001. Ratings of features he had not altered moved with it: physical appearance t = 4.71, mannerisms t = 4.06 and accent t = 3.78, each on df of 1/117. A follow-up showed 34 further students the tapes without sound, and appearance and mannerisms then differed between the two versions with t below 1 for both, which is the paper's ground for treating the attributes as constant. Subjects denied the influence. Of 34 asked whether their liking had shifted their attribute ratings, a majority said it had not, and none of the six distributions differed from the no-effect point. Of 56 asked the reverse question, those who had seen the cold instructor said their view of his appearance, mannerisms and accent had lowered their liking, t = 3.28, 2.80 and 2.74, all p < .01. The physical attractiveness branch of the literature is separate and larger: it asks whether attractive people are credited with traits unrelated to looks, and Eagly and colleagues reviewed it meta-analytically under the title "What is beautiful is good, but...", where the qualification carries the finding. Their abstract reports the gap between attractive and unattractive targets as largest for social competence, intermediate for potency, adjustment and intellectual competence, and near zero for integrity and concern for others.

replication.headline: The phenomenon is old and widely reproduced, and the way it has been measured for most of a century has been argued to be broken.
replication.detail: Murphy, Jako and Anhalt set out the definition of halo error that dominated the twentieth century in four parts: that it was common, that it was a rater error with true and illusory components, that it inflated correlations among rating dimensions through a general evaluation, and that its consequences were bad. Their abstract says all of the major elements of that conception are either wrong or problematic, and calls for a moratorium on using halo indices as dependent measures in applied research. That is a criticism of the construct rather than of the observation. The difficulty is the one built into Thorndike's original argument: calling a correlation between rated traits an error requires knowing what the true correlation is, and in most applied settings nobody does. So an entry cannot honestly say the halo effect replicated or failed. What can be said is that impressions bleed across judgements, that this is easy to demonstrate experimentally where the true answer is fixed by the design, and that the applied measure of halo error in performance appraisal does not rest on solid ground.

study.cite: Murphy, K. R., Jako, R. A., & Anhalt, R. L. (1993). Nature and consequences of halo error: A critical analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 78(2), 218-225.

limits: No standardised effect sizes are printed here. Thorndike reports correlations, and Nisbett and Wilson report t values and a figure whose bars carry the percentages. The Eagly meta-analysis stayed behind a paywall on this pass as well: Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar and open-web searches produced its record and its abstract but no copy of the article. Its per-trait effect sizes are therefore still named as existing rather than quoted, and the ordering given above is the abstract's own wording rather than a set of numbers. The full text of Murphy, Jako and Anhalt was also not obtained, and their argument is summarised here from their abstract. Both gaps are recorded rather than papered over with figures from a secondary source. The mixed verdict also covers two literatures that are usually run together: impression contamination in experiments, and halo error in workplace ratings. They have different evidence and different problems.
misreadings: The halo effect is often stated as though attractiveness causes people to be judged better at everything, which the meta-analytic title already qualifies: the gap it produces is largest for social competence and near zero for integrity and concern for others. It is also used interchangeably with the horn effect, its negative counterpart, though the two have not been shown to be symmetrical. And in business writing it has drifted into meaning any spillover of reputation between products, which is a different claim about brands rather than a finding about how raters rate people.
